--- title: "The exercise" subtitle: "Independent" bibliography: [../../references.bib, ../../references-new.bib] --- The [background page](../../background.qmd) presents the original study, the SCORE replication and the five reanalyses of the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. The independent format takes all six tasks, and you do them in the workspace, which stage 1 installs and which you open in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.). The [browser lab](../../lab.qmd), on which R runs inside your browser, holds every task as well, with hints and worked solutions, and it carries the work if your installation fails. Stage 1 takes Task 1, stage 3 Tasks 2 and 3, and stage 4 Tasks 4 to 6. Sending your results to the class chart is optional. --- ## The claim Five independent analysts reanalysed one claim of the original authors (OAs) [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] in the robustness study. The claim, as the analysts received it, was: > "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" (p. 100 of the published article) The published result behind it is the coefficient of the Hispanic names in a logistic regression of a named greeting on the three groups of names, with community controls and the Hard Email indicator: **−0.82 (standard error 0.22) on 549 replies**, which the OAs translate into a gap of **−20.0 percentage points** in the probability of a named greeting, with a 95% confidence interval from −30.5 to −10.0. The data come from an experiment: 1,014 emails to housing authorities, each of which was signed with one of six names that were assigned at random. ## The five analysts {#the-five-analysts} ::: {#tbl-five .cell tbl-cap='The five reanalyses, with the statistic recorded in the robustness study and the gap in percentage points by the course refit. Source: `data/analysts5.csv`.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Analyst Comparison Emails counted Recorded statistic Gap (points) Conclusion in Task 1
8PTRZ Hispanic against other names replies χ2 = 14.265 −17.3 evidence for the claim
UYV3F Hispanic against white names replies z = −3.771 −20.0 evidence for the claim
EWFMI Hispanic against white names (three-group model) replies z = 3.645 −19.4 evidence for the claim
25N5D Hispanic against white names all delivered emails χ2 = 13.683 −13.2 no evidence either way
P9W8Y three groups replies none recorded −20.0 no evidence either way
``` ::: ::: All five found Hispanic names greeted by name less often than the comparison names, and all four recorded statistics reproduce exactly on the public file. Two of the five nevertheless concluded in Task 1 of the robustness study that the data showed no evidence either way, and the [background page](../../background.qmd#sec-reanalysts) sets out what question each analyst answered. --- ## The tasks The exercise runs as six numbered tasks, and the report of the workspace, `index.qmd`, holds the steps of each. ### Task 1 – The setup check Open the workspace folder in your IDE and run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, which prints OK when everything is in place and otherwise says what is missing. ### Task 2 – The data, the estimand and the graph First, count what came back for each name in the 1,014 emails of `housing_emails.csv` ([codebook](../../data/housing_emails_codebook.md)): the emails that bounced, the replies, and the replies that opened with the name of the sender. Second, write the **estimand statement** behind the claim. It says which comparison is made (Hispanic names against which names), which emails are counted (the replies, or every delivered email), and which outcome is compared. The [specification menu](../../menu.qmd) gives the template. Third, finish the **causal graph**. The graph shows why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name: it compares only the emails that an official chose to answer, and the name may itself have changed that choice, which the [background page](../../background.qmd#sec-posttreatment) calls post-treatment conditioning. It also shows why counting every delivered email keeps the comparison as randomisation made it. ### Task 3 – The reproduction Reproduce the analysis of one of the five analysts in the table above from the public file of the OAs, `housing_original.csv` ([codebook](../../data/housing_original_codebook.md)), in the tab of that analyst. Then find out why your number is what it is. A reproduction depends on the defaults and the codings of the software as well as on the data and the model. ### Task 4 – The menu This task is **exploratory**: nothing in it is preregistered, and you may look, change your mind and try again. Try several specifications from the [specification menu](../../menu.qmd) with `try_spec()`, one decision at a time, and note which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Then choose the one that you would defend, and `submit_exploration()` sends it to the class chart on the [Class results](../../class-results.qmd) page, where it appears as an open circle. ### Task 5 – Preregistration Choose **one** specification, one option for each decision, and complete the preregistration block **before you run it**. `run_spec()` fits the specification that you declared, and `report_result()` sends the declared result to the class chart, where it appears as a filled circle. Then find where your result sits on the curve of 64 specifications. Task 4 and Task 5 run the same code. An exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit both so that the two sets of class results can be compared. ### Task 6 – Replication Fit the specification that you declared in Task 5 on the data of the SCORE replication, a new experiment of 2020 with four new male names, `housing_replication.csv` ([codebook](../../data/housing_replication_codebook.md)). `replicate_spec()` translates the specification to the design of the new experiment, which had no Black names, no reply without a greeting code and no indicator of a hard-to-find address, and prints each change. Then place the result on the curve of the claim on the new data, beside its place on the curve of the original data. ### Your own project Stage 5 asks a question beyond the claim, one that the data of the case study support, and fixes its preregistration with a date that someone else can check before anything in it runs. The page of [stage 5](stage-5.qmd) lists the projects that the case study supports. --- ## What counts as a result A result counts for the class chart if it is one of the 64 specifications on the curve, if it reaches the chart through `submit_exploration()` or `report_result()`, which fill in the class-results form for you, and if it comes with a written reason for each choice; two sentences are enough. The reasons are what make a set of different results more than a spread of numbers, because they show which differences between results come from different questions and which from different ways of answering the same one. --- ## Links The tools of the route: - [Setup](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html) - [Setup help](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/help.html) - [The workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing-workspace/) – the report as it renders - [Browser lab](../../lab.qmd) - [Slides](../day/slides.qmd) – the deck used in the day format The pages of the case study: - [Background](../../background.qmd) - [Specification menu](../../menu.qmd) - [Decision map](../../menu.qmd#map) - [Specification curve](../../curve.qmd) - [Class results](../../class-results.qmd)
